summary: BBN suggests adding a restart procedure to the File Transfer Protocol. Remote job service sites commonly handle very long files, such as hundreds of pages of printer output, so a failed transfer should be able to resume near where it stopped instead of starting over.

plainLanguage.summary: If downloading a huge file breaks halfway, you should not have to start from the beginning. This note suggests a way to pick up where you left off.

questions: how can file transfers resume on the arpanet
why did large files need restart capability
how do sequence numbers help recover broken transfers
subtitle: A proposal to add restart capability to the File Transfer Protocol

tldr.problem: File transfers over the ARPANET could be hundreds of pages long (like printer output), but if the connection failed partway through, the entire transfer had to restart from the beginning, wasting bandwidth and time.
tldr.mechanism: BBN proposed four new opcodes for FTP: Append at sequence number, Retrieve at sequence number, Resume Retrieve, and Use the sequence number. These let sender and receiver agree on where to resume a broken transfer using sequence numbers as restart markers.
tldr.outcome: Sites like UCLA-CCN agreed to implement these commands if accepted by the working group, storing sequence numbers with files on disk to enable reliable restarts.

today: RFC 281 is a proposal for FTP enhancement. It updates RFC 265 and remains an important historical record of how the ARPANET community addressed practical file transfer challenges.

sections.title: The Problem: Long File Transfers
sections.content:
RFC 281 addresses a practical problem discovered during remote job service discussions. While early ARPANET applications dealt with small transmissions (a few characters, a line, or a page), remote job services at UCLA-CCN and UCSB routinely handled much larger files. Printer output files commonly exceeded 400 pages.

Without a restart capability, a transmission failure partway through meant starting the entire multi-page transfer again. BBN (the ARPANET contractor) proposed adding restart capability to the File Transfer Protocol to address this need.
sections.plainLanguage: The early network was designed for short messages. But real users needed to send huge files like printer output. If something broke, starting over wasted everyone's time.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers as Restart Markers
sections.content:
The proposal uses two existing features in the underlying Data Transfer Protocol: information separators and sequence numbers. After discussion, the group chose sequence numbers as unambiguous markers for restart locations. This meant some hosts like TIPs that don't use sequence numbering would be excluded from this recovery mechanism, but it solved the problem for full hosts.

The critical insight is that both sender and receiver must agree exactly where the restart begins. Sequence numbers provide that agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: They decided to mark each piece of data with a number. If the connection breaks, both sides can agree to start at number 50 (or wherever they got to).

sections.title: Four New FTP Commands
sections.content:
RFC 281 proposes four new opcodes (each with a hex code). Append at sequence number (0x10) and Retrieve at sequence number (0x11) let one side propose a restart point. The other side either agrees or responds with Use this sequence number (0x13) if it cannot restart at that location. Resume Retrieve (0x12) is used when the receiver doesn't care about the exact sequence number and lets the server pick a restart point.

These commands handle three scenarios: user sending when the path breaks, user receiving and unconcerned with the exact restart point, and user receiving and concerned about the exact location. Multiple fallback options handle cases where one side cannot perform the requested restart.
sections.plainLanguage: The four commands are: ask to restart here, ask to restart here for receiving, let the server pick where to restart, and suggest a different restart point.

sections.title: Acceptance and Implementation
sections.content:
The proposal notes that UCLA-CCN and UCSB agreed in principle to implement these commands if accepted by the Network Working Group. Implementation would require storing sequence numbers with files on non-volatile storage so that restarts could be reliably effected even after system failures.

This RFC is essentially a proposal for the FTP committee to consider, inviting comments or counter-proposals. It represents practical engineering addressing real operational needs on the early ARPANET.
sections.plainLanguage: The big sites agreed to use this if everyone else did. They would write the restart information to disk so it survives even if the computer crashes.
